must.text: Makes the main diagnosis: each poll returns more work than one consumer finishes within the 30-second acquisition lock, and in the default implicit mode the records are only acknowledged at the next poll, so the locks expire and the same records are delivered again to other consumers, which renders them again.

Says max.poll.records=5 has no effect here because the default share.acquire.mode=batch_optimized lets poll() return more records than max.poll.records; only share.acquire.mode=record_limit enforces it.
Confirms read-only with the broker metric kafka.server:type=SharePartitionMetrics,name=AcquisitionLockTimeoutPerSec for group pdf-render (non-zero means locks expire before acknowledgement).
Confirms read-only by logging how many records each poll() returns and how long processing that batch takes, and comparing it with the 30-second lock.

Bounds the work per poll so that it finishes inside the lock: sets share.acquire.mode=record_limit together with a small max.poll.records (number of records x worst-case render time below the lock duration).

If a longer lock is wanted, raises share.record.lock.duration.ms for this group only, as a group configuration: kafka-configs.sh --alter --entity-type groups --entity-name pdf-render --add-config share.record.lock.duration.ms=<ms>.

must_not.text: Recommends setting share.record.lock.duration.ms (or group.share.record.lock.duration.ms) in the share consumer's client properties as the fix.
must_not.condition: only if the client properties are named as the place to set it; setting it on the group with kafka-configs.sh, or the broker default in server.properties, does not count
must_not.near_miss: share.record.lock.duration.ms is a group configuration, set with kafka-configs.sh --entity-type groups --entity-name pdf-render.

must_not.text: Recommends raising share.delivery.count.limit as the fix for the duplicate PDFs.
must_not.condition: only if offered as a fix or mitigation for the duplicates; explaining that the limit (5 by default) caps how many times a record is delivered does not count
must_not.near_miss: share.delivery.count.limit (5 by default) caps how many times one record can be delivered, which is why a PDF arrives at most about five times.

reference: The share group hands out records under an acquisition lock of 30 seconds by default. Your consumers use the default implicit acknowledgement mode, so a record is acknowledged only on the next call to poll(). A poll that returns, say, 30 records takes about two minutes to render, so most locks run out first; the broker then releases those records and another consumer gets them and renders them again. That is the duplicates, the wasted CPU and the growing lag; more pods only add more parallel re-deliveries. Setting max.poll.records=5 changed nothing because the default share.acquire.mode=batch_optimized may return more records than max.poll.records to align with batch boundaries. Confirm without changing anything: watch kafka.server:type=SharePartitionMetrics,name=AcquisitionLockTimeoutPerSec for group pdf-render (non-zero means locks expire before acknowledgement), and log the record count per poll and the time each batch takes. Fix: set share.acquire.mode=record_limit with max.poll.records small enough that records x worst render time (8 s) stays well under the lock, for example 2. If you want more headroom, raise the lock for this group only: kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server <b> --alter --entity-type groups --entity-name pdf-render --add-config share.record.lock.duration.ms=60000. The broker caps it at group.share.max.record.lock.duration.ms (60 s by default, read-only, so raising the cap needs a rolling restart). Do not raise share.delivery.count.limit; it would only allow more duplicates.
correct_alternative: Implicit acknowledgement plus big batches: records are acknowledged only when the next poll() happens, and a batch of many 4-second renders outlasts the 30 s acquisition lock, so the locks expire and other consumers receive the same records. max.poll.records is not enforced while share.acquire.mode is batch_optimized. Check first: add a log line with the number of records per poll and the batch duration; you will see batches far beyond 30 s. Then switch the consumers to share.acquire.mode=record_limit with max.poll.records=2, so each poll's work fits in the lock, and roll the pods. Optionally use explicit acknowledgement so each record is acknowledged as soon as it is rendered.
generic: Duplicate processing usually means consumers are too slow or are rebalancing. Check the consumer logs and the group with kafka-share-groups.sh, give the pods more CPU and memory, and make your processing idempotent so duplicates do not matter.
note: The renew acknowledgement (design.md:272, share.renew.acknowledge.enable default true) is also a correct way to keep long renders locked; a judge should accept it as an additional fix but it is not a must point because its Java API name is not in the pinned sources. The broker-level default group.share.record.lock.duration.ms (kafka_config.html:1664-1672) is also valid but cluster-wide.

must.text: Makes the main diagnosis: time-based retention uses the largest record timestamp in a segment, so a segment in partitions 4 and 9 that holds gateway records with CreateTime far in the future is not eligible for deletion until that future time plus 72 hours, and the old readings in it stay.

Explains the timing: before 4.0 message.timestamp.after.max.ms had no effective limit, and since 4.0 it defaults to 1 hour, so with CreateTime the brokers now reject records more than an hour in the future; the gateways' 'out of acceptable range' errors are those rejections and the same clock problem.

Confirms read-only on the oldest segment of meter-readings-4 and -9: kafka-dump-log.sh --files <segment>.log shows record batches whose CreateTime (max timestamp) lies in the future, or kafka-get-offsets.sh --topic meter-readings --partitions 4,9 --time max-timestamp locates the record with the largest timestamp.

Removes the stuck data only on partitions 4 and 9 with kafka-delete-records.sh --offset-json-file, giving per partition the first offset that must be kept (the start of the data inside the 72 hours), after checking which offsets that is.
Prevents a repeat by setting message.timestamp.type=LogAppendTime on meter-readings, so broker time is stored and retention no longer depends on gateway clocks.
Prevents a repeat by having the gateway team fix the gateways' clocks, so that the CreateTime timestamps they send are correct.

must_not.text: Recommends raising message.timestamp.after.max.ms (or log.message.timestamp.after.max.ms), for example back to Long.MAX, to make the gateways' send errors go away.
must_not.condition: only if recommended as a change to make; explaining that the 1-hour default rejects the records does not count
must_not.near_miss: The 1-hour default of message.timestamp.after.max.ms, new in 4.0, is what now rejects the gateways' future-dated records.

must_not.text: Recommends lowering retention.ms on meter-readings, even temporarily, to purge the old readings.
must_not.condition: only if recommended as a step; saying that retention.ms=72h is correct does not count
must_not.near_miss: retention.ms stays at 72 hours; it is not the setting at fault, because the stuck segment's largest timestamp lies in the future.

must_not.text: Says the cause for partitions 4 and 9 is an active segment that never rolls and offers lowering segment.ms as the fix.
must_not.condition: only if given as the cause or the fix for partitions 4 and 9; mentioning segment.ms as background does not count
must_not.near_miss: segment.ms decides when the active segment rolls; it does not change when a closed segment expires.

reference: Time-based retention deletes whole segments, and a segment's age is taken from the largest record timestamp in it. With message.timestamp.type at its default, CreateTime, that is the gateway's clock. Some gateways with clocks far ahead wrote readings into partitions 4 and 9 before the upgrade; the segments holding them count as 'new' until that future time plus 72 hours, so the October readings in them stay. Kafka 3.9 accepted such records (message.timestamp.after.max.ms had no effective limit). Since 4.0 the default is 1 hour, so with CreateTime the brokers now reject records more than an hour ahead: that is the 'timestamp out of acceptable range' error on the gateways, the same clock problem. Confirm without changing anything: run kafka-dump-log.sh --files on the oldest .log segment of meter-readings-4 and -9 and look at the CreateTime values of the batches, or kafka-get-offsets.sh --topic meter-readings --partitions 4,9 --time max-timestamp. To become compliant, delete only what is held: kafka-delete-records.sh --bootstrap-server <b> --offset-json-file del.json, with partitions 4 and 9 and, for each, the first offset that is within the 72 hours. Check the offsets before running it; it moves the log start offset and cannot be undone. Lowering retention.ms would not free that segment and would delete good data elsewhere. To keep it that way, fix the gateway clocks, or set message.timestamp.type=LogAppendTime on the topic so broker time is used; do not raise message.timestamp.after.max.ms to silence the errors.
correct_alternative: The audit is seeing segments that retention cannot expire: retention compares the newest timestamp in a segment with now, and gateways with clocks set into the future put records with such timestamps into partitions 4 and 9. In 4.x those records would be rejected (message.timestamp.after.max.ms is 1 hour by default since 4.0, which is the error the gateways now get), but these came in under 3.9.1. Verify with kafka-get-offsets.sh --time max-timestamp on partitions 4 and 9, then dump that segment with kafka-dump-log.sh. Remove the held data with kafka-delete-records.sh, offsets per partition up to the first record inside the 72 hours. Have the gateway team correct the device clocks so their sends are accepted again.
generic: Retention in Kafka is not exact: segments are only deleted after they roll and the log cleaner runs. Check retention.ms and segment.ms on the topic, make sure the brokers have the right configuration, and wait for the next retention check.
note: Neither the Kafka documentation on disk nor the index describes kafka-dump-log on data segments, kafka-get-offsets --time max-timestamp or kafka-delete-records; m3 and m4 rest on the tool sources only. The chunk title of 0b8671328a3ed515 says 4.0.1 but upgrade.md:336 sits under 'Notable changes in 4.0.0'. The rubric does not judge whether the result satisfies any law.

Fixes it by removing the override so the brokers' message.max.bytes applies: kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server <b> --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name scans --delete-config max.message.bytes.
Says to change max.message.bytes in the Terraform module too, or the next apply puts the 1 MB override back.

reference: The broker change did nothing for this topic because scans has its own max.message.bytes=1048588, a topic-level override that the Terraform module set when it created the topic; the synonyms line shows it as DYNAMIC_TOPIC_CONFIG above the STATIC_BROKER_CONFIG. A broker's message.max.bytes is only the default for topics without an override. The limit applies to the record batch after compression, so small or compressible documents pass and the large scans, which compress poorly, are rejected with MESSAGE_TOO_LARGE. Fix: kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name scans --add-config max.message.bytes=8388608. Then change the same setting in the Terraform module, or the next apply restores 1 MB. The changes to replica.fetch.max.bytes and the consumers' max.partition.fetch.bytes were not needed: neither is an absolute maximum, and a first batch larger than them is still returned. max.request.size at 8 MB is fine. Verify with kafka-configs.sh --describe --entity-type topics --entity-name scans and by resending the 6.1 MB contract.
correct_alternative: Your topic carries an explicit max.message.bytes=1048588 (DYNAMIC_TOPIC_CONFIG in the describe output). Per-topic overrides win over the broker's message.max.bytes, so the 8 MB broker value is never used for scans. Remove the override so the topic falls back to the broker value: kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name scans --delete-config max.message.bytes, and drop the setting from the Terraform resource. The check is on the compressed batch, which is why only big scans fail. Describe the topic again to see the override gone, then resend the failed document.
generic: RecordTooLargeException means the message is too big. Increase the size limits on the producer, broker and consumer, or compress or split large messages, or store large files in object storage and send a reference.
note: Storing the files elsewhere and sending a reference is a valid design choice but does not answer why the broker change had no effect; it is not a must-not. The exception class and its message in the evidence come from the Java client and are not in the pinned sources; the message text matches MESSAGE_TOO_LARGE in protocol_errors.html:18.

Adds a PREFIXED ACL for the ids: kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server <b> --command-config admin.properties --add --allow-principal User:settlement --operation Write --operation Describe --transactional-id settlement- --resource-pattern-type prefixed.
Adds LITERAL Write and Describe ACLs on each of the three transactional ids settlement-0, settlement-1 and settlement-2.
Says the IdempotentWrite ACL on the cluster does not help here (a producer authorised on its transactional id gets idempotence anyway) and can be removed.
Says that sending the consumed offsets to the transaction also needs Read on group settlement, and that this ACL is already present.
Verifies with kafka-acls.sh --list --transactional-id settlement-0 --resource-pattern-type match (shows literal, wildcard and prefixed ACLs that apply) and by restarting one pod.

reference: The ticket gave the ACL on the transactional id settlement with the default pattern type, LITERAL. A literal ACL only matches a resource with exactly that name, but your pods use settlement-0, settlement-1 and settlement-2. A transactional producer needs Describe on its transactional id to find the transaction coordinator and Write to initialise and run transactions, so initTransactions fails with TRANSACTIONAL_ID_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED. The IdempotentWrite ACL your colleague added is not the missing permission: a producer authorised on its transactional id gets idempotence anyway, so you can remove it. Add one prefixed ACL: kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9093 --command-config admin.properties --add --allow-principal User:settlement --operation Write --operation Describe --transactional-id settlement- --resource-pattern-type prefixed. This covers future pods too. Sending the consumed offsets to the transaction also needs Read on group settlement, which you already have, and Read on payments-cleared, also present. Optionally remove the unused literal ACL on settlement. Check with kafka-acls.sh --list --transactional-id settlement-0 --resource-pattern-type match, which shows all ACLs that apply, then restart one pod.
correct_alternative: Your producers' transactional ids are settlement-0/1/2, but the ACL was created for the literal id settlement, which matches nothing else. Grant the three ids explicitly: kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9093 --command-config admin.properties --add --allow-principal User:settlement --operation Write --operation Describe --transactional-id settlement-0 --transactional-id settlement-1 --transactional-id settlement-2. If you later scale the StatefulSet, add the new id or switch to a prefixed pattern. The cluster IdempotentWrite grant is unrelated; the transactional id grant is what initTransactions needs. Restart a pod and confirm it starts.
generic: An authorization error means the user lacks permissions. Check the ACLs with kafka-acls.sh --list, make sure the user has the right permissions on the topics, group and cluster, and check the SASL credentials of the client.

must.text: Says that acks=1 conflicts with idempotence and that, because enable.idempotence is not set explicitly, the producer silently disables idempotence, so retries can write duplicates.
Sets acks=all (the default), because with acks=1 a record acknowledged by the leader is lost if the leader fails before the followers have it.
Sets enable.idempotence=true explicitly, so that a conflicting setting fails with a ConfigException instead of silently turning idempotence off.
Rejects max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=10 and keeps it at 5 or less (5 is the default), because idempotence requires at most 5 requests in flight.
Flags delivery.timeout.ms=20000 as below request.timeout.ms + linger.ms (30020 ms) and sets it at least to that sum, or leaves the 120000 default.
Removes retries=3 (leaves the default) and bounds retrying with delivery.timeout.ms instead.

must_not.text: Says idempotence is active with these settings because enable.idempotence defaults to true.
must_not.condition: whenever stated about this configuration
must_not.near_miss: enable.idempotence defaults to true only when no conflicting settings are made.

must_not.text: Says max.in.flight.requests.per.connection must be 1 to keep per-key ordering with an idempotent producer.
must_not.condition: only if stated as required; choosing 1 as a cautious option without calling it required does not count
must_not.near_miss: Without idempotence, more than one request in flight with retries can reorder records.

reference: As written this producer is not idempotent. Idempotence is on by default only when nothing conflicts with it; acks=1 conflicts, and because enable.idempotence is not set explicitly the client silently disables it. Retries can then write duplicates. acks=1 also breaks the durability requirement: the leader acknowledges before the followers have the record, so a leader failure right after the acknowledgement loses it. Use acks=all; with min.insync.replicas=2 a write is acknowledged only when two replicas have it. Set enable.idempotence=true explicitly: then any conflicting setting fails at startup with a ConfigException instead of quietly turning idempotence off. Do not raise max.in.flight.requests.per.connection to 10: idempotence needs 5 or less, it keeps per-key ordering for any value up to 5, and since Kafka 4.0 the producer no longer falls back to non-idempotent when the value is above 5. delivery.timeout.ms=20000 is below request.timeout.ms + linger.ms (30020 ms); the documentation says it should be at least that sum, so leave the 120000 default. Remove retries=3 and let delivery.timeout.ms bound retrying. Suggested: acks=all, enable.idempotence=true, max.in.flight.requests.per.connection unset (5), retries unset, delivery.timeout.ms=120000, request.timeout.ms=30000, linger.ms=20, compression.type=lz4, plus the serializers.
correct_alternative: Remove acks=1, retries=3 and delivery.timeout.ms=20000 so the defaults apply (acks=all, retries at maximum, 120 s delivery timeout), and add enable.idempotence=true. The current file disables idempotence without saying so, because acks=1 conflicts with it and the setting is not explicit; it also risks losing acknowledged writes on a leader failure. The delivery timeout is shorter than request.timeout.ms plus linger.ms, which the docs say it must not be. Keep max.in.flight.requests.per.connection at 5: higher values are not allowed with idempotence, and Kafka 4.x no longer quietly drops idempotence for them. Ordering per account is kept with 5 in flight.
generic: For reliable producing, enable retries, use compression and tune linger.ms and batch.size for throughput. Monitor producer metrics such as record-error-rate and request-latency-avg, and test failover before going live.
note: Whether the Java producer refuses to start with delivery.timeout.ms below request.timeout.ms + linger.ms is not in the pinned sources; the rubric only requires the documented constraint. The 4.0 note (upgrade.md:304) and the enable.idempotence description (producer_config.html:643-644) read differently for max.in.flight above 5 without an explicit setting; m4 accepts either 'fails' or 'not allowed'.

must.text: Says byte-rate quotas are enforced per broker, so producer_byte_rate=62914560 lets analytics produce up to about 360 MB/s across 6 brokers, and divides every cluster target by the broker count (about 10 MB/s per broker for analytics, 2 MB/s for the bulk loader, 5 MB/s for the default).
Says the client-id quota for bulk-loader never applies to analytics' connections, because a matching user quota (precedence 3) wins over a matching client-id quota (precedence 7).

Says the (analytics, bulk-loader) quota is a separate quota group from the analytics user quota, so analytics' total is the sum of both, and lowers the user quota to the remainder (about 48 MB/s, so about 8 MB/s per broker) to keep the total near 60 MB/s.
Says the per-broker figures assume the analytics traffic is spread evenly over the brokers' partition leaders; with skew a client is throttled on one broker before reaching the cluster total.
Verifies the new quotas with kafka-configs.sh --describe on the same entities, for example --entity-type users --entity-name analytics --entity-type clients --entity-name bulk-loader.

Sets the bulk loader's quota on the (user, client-id) pair instead: kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config 'producer_byte_rate=<per-broker value>' --entity-type users --entity-name analytics --entity-type clients --entity-name bulk-loader.

must_not.text: Says producer_byte_rate is a cluster-wide total for the user or client.
must_not.condition: whenever stated
must_not.near_miss: Each broker enforces the quota on the traffic it receives.

must_not.text: Says a client-id quota takes precedence over a user quota for the same connection.
must_not.condition: whenever stated
must_not.near_miss: A (user, client-id) quota is the most specific match and wins over the user quota.

reference:
Two problems. First, quotas are per broker: each broker lets a quota group produce up to the configured rate, so 62914560 bytes/s for analytics allows about 360 MB/s across your 6 brokers. Divide each cluster target by six, which assumes the traffic is spread evenly over the partition leaders; with skew, clients hit the limit on one broker first. Second, the bulk-loader line does nothing for analytics. For a connection the most specific matching quota applies, in the order (user, client-id), user with default client-id, user, ... and only then client-id. analytics has a user quota, so its bulk-loader connections use that and the client-id quota is ignored. Put it on the pair. Note that the pair is then its own quota group: the bulk loader no longer counts against the analytics user quota, so lower that to the remainder. Corrected:
--alter --add-config 'producer_byte_rate=8388608' --entity-type users --entity-name analytics
--alter --add-config 'producer_byte_rate=2097152' --entity-type users --entity-name analytics --entity-type clients --entity-name bulk-loader
--alter --add-config 'producer_byte_rate=5242880' --entity-type users --entity-default
These take effect without a restart. Check with --describe on the same entities and on the brokers' kafka.server:type=Produce,user=analytics,client-id=bulk-loader throttle-time and byte-rate metrics.
correct_alternative: Quotas count per broker, not per cluster, so with six brokers analytics would get six times 60 MB/s; use about 10 MB/s per broker for analytics and 5 MB/s for the user default. The bulk-loader quota as written is a client-id quota, which ranks below the user quota in the precedence order, so it never applies to analytics. Set it as a (user, client-id) quota of about 2 MB/s per broker with --entity-type users --entity-name analytics --entity-type clients --entity-name bulk-loader. Then the loader has its own 12 MB/s and the rest of analytics shares the user quota, so analytics can reach about 70 MB/s in total; if 60 is a hard ceiling, give the user quota 8 MB/s per broker. Watch the throttle-time of the Produce quota metrics afterwards.
generic: Kafka supports quotas on users and client ids with kafka-configs.sh. Set producer_byte_rate and consumer_byte_rate for each team according to your capacity plan and monitor throttling.
note: m3 is inferred from 'the most specific quota matching the connection is applied' and 'All connections of a quota group share the quota' (design.md:478); the docs do not state the sum, so its chunk holds the premises only (second review: partial). Numbers accept a tolerance of about 10 %; 10 MB/s for analytics is accepted in m1 when m3 is not made. The second review split the old m2 into the cause (m2) and the fix (m6).

must.text: Configures the consumer with enable.auto.commit=false and no longer commits offsets through the consumer.
Configures the producer with a transactional.id that is unique per pod (for example derived from the pod name) and calls initTransactions() once before the loop.

Sends the consumed positions (the offset of the next record to read, per partition) to the transaction with producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(...) before commitTransaction(), so that the output records and the offsets commit or abort together.
Tells billing to set isolation.level=read_committed on its consumers, because with the default read_uncommitted they also see records of aborted transactions.
On an abortable error, calls abortTransaction() and rewinds the consumer to the last committed offsets (committed() and seek()) or recreates the consumer, so the aborted records are processed again.

On an error after which the producer must be restarted (an application-recoverable error, for example the producer being fenced because another instance uses the same transactional.id), closes the producer and recreates it or stops, instead of aborting and carrying on with the same producer.

must_not.text: Also commits the processed offsets with consumer.commitSync() or commitAsync() in the transactional loop.
must_not.condition: only if the consumer commit is part of the proposed loop; mentioning that the old code committed through the consumer does not count
must_not.near_miss: The offsets are committed through producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction, as part of the transaction.

must_not.text: Calls sendOffsetsToTransaction with a String group id (sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, "enricher")).
must_not.condition: whenever the code or text uses the String overload
must_not.near_miss: sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, consumer.groupMetadata()).

correct_alternative: Use the transactional producer with one producer per consumer. Set transactional.id from the pod's stable name and call initTransactions() at start. In the loop: poll, beginTransaction(), send the enriched records, build the map of next offsets (last offset + 1 per partition) and pass it with consumer.groupMetadata() to sendOffsetsToTransaction(), then commitTransaction(). On any KafkaException other than fencing, the simplest safe policy is to close producer and consumer and create them again: the group rebalances and the consumer starts from the last committed offsets. On ProducerFencedException stop the pod's loop. Consumer config: enable.auto.commit=false. Billing's consumers need isolation.level=read_committed.
generic: To avoid duplicates, enable idempotence on the producer and make your consumers idempotent. Commit offsets after processing, handle exceptions with retries, and monitor consumer lag.
note: The design page (design.md:244) allows recreating producer and consumer instead of seeking; m5 accepts either. The 4.3 docs name error categories (design.md:231-238) rather than ProducerFencedException; the tool source TransactionalMessageCopier.java:400 uses ProducerFencedException. An answer that names the categories (abort on abortable errors, restart the producer on application-recoverable ones) meets m5 and m6.

must.text: Turns off the default auto-commit (enable.auto.commit=false) and commits offsets explicitly, because auto-commit commits the consumer's position in the background whether or not the INSERT has finished, which is how the 37 invoices were lost. An answer that keeps auto-commit on but lets it commit only offsets the code has explicitly marked as written to Postgres also meets this point.
Commits a partition's offset only after the Postgres transaction for the records up to that offset has committed (process first, then save the position).
With parallel workers, commits per partition only up to the highest offset below which every record is done (no gaps), or processes each partition's records in order.
Commits the offset of the next record to read, that is the last processed offset + 1.

reference:
The loss comes from auto-commit: enable.auto.commit defaults to true and commits the consumer's position in the background, whether or not the work handed to the pool has reached Postgres. The drained pod was killed with INSERTs still queued, the group resumed after them, so lag was 0 and 37 invoices were never written.
1. Set enable.auto.commit=false and commit offsets yourself, synchronously.
2. Simplest correct loop, without the pool: take a batch from the consumer, write it to Postgres in one database transaction with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (invoice_id) DO NOTHING, commit that transaction, and only then commit the batch's Kafka offsets. The committed offset is the next record to read: last written offset + 1 per partition. A crash between the two commits only replays the batch, and the unique invoice_id absorbs the duplicate.
3. If you keep the pool for throughput: per partition, track which offsets have committed in Postgres and commit only up to the highest offset below which every record is done, + 1, never past a gap. When partitions are revoked, wait for their in-flight INSERTs and commit their finished offsets before the revocation completes, so the next owner repeats little.
A rebalance then cannot lose an invoice: anything not committed is delivered again, and the ON CONFLICT clause makes the replay harmless.
correct_alternative: Keep the 8 workers but make commits follow completed work. Configure the consumer with enable.auto.commit set to false. Each worker returns (partition, offset) when its INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE has committed. The poll thread keeps, per partition, the set of finished offsets and advances a watermark to the highest offset with no gap below it; every second it commits watermark + 1 for each partition with a synchronous commit. In the revoke callback it pauses, waits for the futures of the revoked partitions, commits their watermarks synchronously and then returns. A crash replays at most the uncommitted tail, which the upsert absorbs.

reference: Per second, with leaders spread evenly over the zones: producers reach a leader in another zone 2/3 of the time, about 100 MB/s; the four consumer groups fetch from leaders, 2/3 of them in another zone, 4 x 150 x 2/3 = about 400 MB/s; replication sends each byte to two followers, up to 2 x 150 = 300 MB/s across zones (exactly that once every partition has one replica per zone; today it depends on the placement). So today up to about 800 MB/s, about half of it consumer fetches. Remove that half with follower fetching, in this order: 1) broker.rack=<zone> on every broker (read-only, rolling restart); 2) find partitions without a replica in every zone (kafka-topics.sh --describe) and reassign them with throttled kafka-reassign-partitions.sh plans, because setting broker.rack does not move existing replicas; 3) replica.selector.class=org.apache.kafka.common.replica.RackAwareReplicaSelector on the brokers (read-only, rolling restart); 4) client.rack=<zone> on every consumer. Consumers then read from the in-zone replica and fall back to the leader when there is none. Result about 400 MB/s (100 produce + 300 replication); if some followers now share their leader's zone, step 2 adds a little replication traffic. Do not lower the replication factor: replication is the price of surviving a zone loss. Trade-off: a follower serves records only after it has them, so end-to-end latency rises; how much that matters depends on your consumers' latency budget, which you did not give, nor the price per GB.
correct_alternative: Most of the bill is consumers fetching from leaders: four groups x 150 MB/s x 2/3 cross-zone is about 400 of the up to roughly 800 MB/s that crosses zones (the rest is about 100 MB/s of produce traffic and up to 300 MB/s of replication, depending on today's placement). Before switching consumers, make sure every partition has one replica per zone, reassigning those that do not, because racks only guide placement when replicas are created or moved. Expect total cross-zone traffic near 400 MB/s. Consumers will lag a little behind leader reads, so confirm the latency budget first.
generic: To reduce cross-zone costs, review your topology, compress messages, shorten retention where possible and monitor network usage per broker. Consider placing clients close to the brokers they use.

The computed point assumes the producers' and consumers' figures are on-wire (compressed) bytes and that leaders are spread evenly over zones. Today's replication traffic across zones depends on the arbitrary placement (at most 300 MB/s); the second review dropped the old m6 for that reason and because the rubric had 7 must points.

reference:
Two separate causes.

1. nightly-reconciler: your template sets showAllOffsets: false. With that, Kafka Exporter stops collecting metrics for groups whose consumers are disconnected; by default it reports every group regardless of connection status. When the CronJob died at 01:10 the group had no connected member, so its kafka_consumergroup_lag series vanished and the alert had nothing to evaluate. Set showAllOffsets: true (or delete the line) under spec.kafkaExporter in the Kafka resource core.

2. billing-sync: Kafka Exporter computes lag from the offsets committed to __consumer_offsets. billing-sync uses assign() and stores its offsets in Postgres, never committing them to Kafka, so there is nothing to report. If you want its lag in the same dashboards, have it also commit its processed offsets to its group in Kafka; Postgres can stay its source of truth.

The filters are not involved: groupRegex ".*" matches both groups and groupExcludeRegex "^(console-consumer|tmp)-.*" matches neither.

To see last night's real backlog now, run bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server <bootstrap> --describe --group nightly-reconciler: it shows CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET and LAG per partition. Do not delete or reset the group to make metrics reappear. Broker JMX metrics do not carry group lag, so changing metricsConfig will not help.
correct_alternative: The exporter template hides disconnected groups: showAllOffsets: false means a group with no connected consumers gets no metrics, which is exactly the state of nightly-reconciler after its crash, so the series ended and the alert stayed silent. Remove the setting (the default reports all consumers) or set it to true in spec.kafkaExporter. billing-sync is invisible for another reason: the exporter only knows offsets committed to __consumer_offsets, and that service keeps its offsets in Postgres. Rather than changing how it commits, alert on its own client metric records-lag-max (kafka.consumer:type=consumer-fetch-manager-metrics), which the consumer publishes itself. The regex filters do not exclude either group. Check the nightly backlog with kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group nightly-reconciler.

      matchLabels:
        app: recon-worker
  - namespaceSelector:

      matchLabels:

reference:
Two separate effects.

First, the JVM does not register in-place memory changes. payments-brokers-3 now has 16Gi without a restart, but its JVM runs with the heap it started with. You set no jvmOptions, so Strimzi chose the heap from the old 8Gi limit: 50 %, the 4096M in your GC log. The extra memory only helps the page cache.

Second, a restart alone would not help much: Strimzi's default Kafka heap is 50 % of the memory limit but at most 5 GB. Set the heap explicitly, for example in the brokers KafkaNodePool:

jvmOptions:
  "-Xms": "8g"
  "-Xmx": "8g"

That leaves the rest of the 16Gi for non-heap memory and page cache. A new heap size applies only when a broker restarts, so let Strimzi roll the brokers; do not delete several broker pods at once, and do not set -Xmx to 16g or more.

payments-brokers-5 is a different problem. Its spec shows the new values but status.containerStatuses still shows 2 CPU / 8Gi, and the PodResizePending condition with reason Deferred means the node lacks free capacity now; the kubelet retries. Because the Kafka resource has strimzi.io/in-place-resizing-wait-for-deferred, Strimzi waits indefinitely instead of rolling it. Free capacity on that node, or restart that one pod (a manual rolling update) so it comes back with the new resources.
correct_alternative: In-place resizing gave the containers 16Gi, but a running JVM never sees in-place memory changes, so the heap is still the 4 GiB chosen at start (half of 8Gi). Even a restart would only reach Strimzi's default cap of 5 GB, because no jvmOptions are set. Put -Xms and -Xmx (for example 6g to 8g) into jvmOptions of the node pool, keeping well under 16Gi, and accept that the brokers must restart for it to apply. Broker 5 has not been resized at all: the kubelet marked the resize Deferred for lack of node capacity, and the wait-for-deferred annotation tells Strimzi to wait instead of rolling. reference:
Not as written. A toleration only lets the brokers onto nodes tainted dedicated=kafka:NoSchedule; it does not attract them, so the scheduler can still place brokers on your general nodes. The taint keeps others off, the toleration lets brokers in, and node affinity keeps brokers on those nodes. Add the affinity next to the toleration in the same pool template:

spec:
  template:
    pod:
      tolerations:
        - key: dedicated
          operator: Equal
          value: kafka
          effect: NoSchedule
      affinity:
        nodeAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            nodeSelectorTerms:
              - matchExpressions:
                  - key: node-group
                    operator: In
                    values:
                      - kafka-io

Two more points. NoSchedule does not evict pods that were already running: the batch pods stay until you move them off (delete them so they reschedule elsewhere, or drain the nodes one at a time), or until you use a NoExecute taint. The log shipper is a DaemonSet; it only gets a fixed set of tolerations automatically, none for dedicated=kafka, so add that toleration to its pod template if it must keep running on these nodes, or a re-created log-shipper pod will not be scheduled there. Check placement afterwards with kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -o wide.

Existing batch pods were not evicted by the NoSchedule taint; delete them so they land elsewhere. No. The PR cannot shrink the volumes: decreasing a persistent volume is not supported in Kubernetes, and Strimzi only supports increasing size. The delete-pod-and-pvc cycle is a recovery tool for storage failures, to be used only after non-destructive options; deleting each broker's PVC throws its data away and relies on re-replication six times in a row, with every partition losing a replica each time.

Use the documented node-pool migration, which works because brokers is a broker-only pool and Cruise Control is deployed:

1. Revert the change to the brokers pool. Create a new pool, for example brokers-st1: roles [broker], replicas 6, JBOD volume id 0, persistent-claim, size 800Gi, class st1.
2. Wait until its pods are Ready.
3. Create a KafkaRebalance (label strimzi.io/cluster) with mode: remove-brokers and brokers: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Wait for ProposalReady, approve it with kubectl annotate kafkarebalance <name> strimzi.io/rebalance="approve", and wait for Ready. Cruise Control moves every replica to the new brokers.
4. Only then delete the old pool: kubectl delete kafkanodepool brokers.

Capacity check: about 6 x 420 GB = 2.5 TB of data on 6 x 800Gi (about 5.2 TB), roughly half full, so the new pool has room. Order matters: the old pool is removed only once its brokers hold no replicas.

With Cruise Control you can shrink inside the existing pool instead: revert the change to volume 0 and add a second JBOD volume to the brokers pool, id 1, persistent-claim, size 800Gi, class st1. Then create a KafkaRebalance with mode remove-disks and moveReplicasOffVolumes listing brokerId 0 to 5, each with volumeIds [0]; wait for ProposalReady, approve it and wait for Ready. Only after that remove volume 0 from the pool (the KRaft metadata log then moves to volume 1, which rolls the brokers) and delete the old 2000Gi PVCs yourself, since deleteClaim is false. Do not copy the ingress listener: in Strimzi 1.3.1 type: ingress is deprecated because the Ingress NGINX Controller was archived in March 2026. Use a tlsroute listener, which publishes Kafka through Kubernetes Gateway API TLSRoute resources routed by SNI on one port, 443.

End-to-end mTLS needs TLS passthrough on the Gateway listener: the Gateway forwards the encrypted stream and the brokers see the client certificates. With TLS terminated at the Gateway the listener would be tls: false, clients would see the Gateway's certificate, and client authentication with the brokers is not available.

Outside Strimzi: a Gateway API implementation that supports gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 TLSRoute, and a Gateway with a passthrough listener on 443 that accepts routes from the Kafka namespace; Strimzi manages the routes, not the Gateway. Strimzi creates a ClusterIP service and a TLSRoute for the bootstrap and for each broker: 10 for 9 brokers, so 10 hostnames must resolve to the Gateway address in your on-premises DNS. Clients trust the cluster CA (ca.crt from <cluster>-cluster-ca-cert) unless you install your own listener certificates; each application gets a KafkaUser with tls authentication.

In Strimzi 1.3.1 only broker-only node pools can be scaled up or down, and scaling controller nodes in node pools is not supported, so the controllers you start with are the ones you keep; 9 dual-role nodes would also make 9 controllers where 3 or 5 is usual. reference:
The 4 tasks waited for their departed worker. cdc-connect uses incremental cooperative rebalancing (the default). When a worker leaves the group, Connect waits scheduled.rebalance.max.delay.ms, 300000 ms (5 minutes) by default, for it to return; until then its connectors and tasks stay UNASSIGNED, however idle the other workers are. Pod cdc-connect-connect-2 left at 10:02, so its tasks were reassigned at about 10:07, and the pod's return at 10:11 caused the second rebalance. The HTTP 409 at 10:04 is how Connect answers a restart request while a rebalance is in progress; no restart was needed.

Confirm from what you have: the tasks moved at about 10:07, five minutes after the pod left at 10:02 and four minutes before it came back, which is exactly the default delay, and spec.config sets no scheduled.rebalance.max.delay.ms, so the default applies. The status API showed the tasks as UNASSIGNED, not FAILED, during the gap, and the worker logs show the rebalance at about 10:07. FAILED tasks would need a restart; unassigned ones do not.

Change: lower the delay in the KafkaConnect resource, for example spec.config: scheduled.rebalance.max.delay.ms: 60000. This is the off-heap leak of Kafka Streams 4.3.0. The 4.3 upgrade notes say that 4.3.0 has a critical native memory leak in the RocksDB state store layer (KAFKA-20616): column family options and handles are not released, and under task closes such as rebalances the off-heap memory grows until the process is OOM-killed. A flat heap with container memory stepping up at every rebalance is that pattern, and your HPA and deploys make rebalances frequent.

Confirm before changing anything: check that the deployed image really contains kafka-streams 4.3.0, and plot container memory minus heap against rebalance times; the steps should line up.

Fix: upgrade the application's Kafka Streams library to 4.3.1 or later (4.3.1 contains the fix; 4.3.2 is the latest patch on disk). The brokers are not involved. Raising -Xmx does not help, because RocksDB allocates its block cache, index and filter blocks and memtables off-heap; a higher container limit only buys time.

The long restores: since 4.3 a RocksDB store's changelog offset is persisted only when a memtable is flushed or the store is closed cleanly. After an OOM kill the on-disk offset can be stale, the restore consumer seeks out of range (OffsetOutOfRangeException, TaskCorruptedException) and the task is restored from the changelog in full, without data loss. Fewer OOM kills fix most of it.

Afterwards, bound RocksDB memory with a rocksdb.config.setter that shares one block cache and a WriteBufferManager (BoundedMemoryRocksDBConfig), and size the limit above heap plus that bound.
correct_alternative: Heap is flat, so the growth is native memory, and RocksDB lives there: raising -Xmx changes nothing. Kafka Streams 4.3.0 has a known RocksDB off-heap leak (KAFKA-20616) that grows on task closes, which is why memory steps up at every rebalance. Check that your build pulls kafka-streams 4.3.0 and that non-heap memory jumps at rebalances. Then move the application to Kafka Streams 4.3.1 or later; nothing changes on the brokers. The 20 to 40 minute restores follow from the kills: in 4.3 the store's changelog offset is only written at a flush or a clean close, so an OOM kill can leave it stale and Streams re-initializes the task from the changelog (TaskCorruptedException), which is slow but loses nothing. To keep memory predictable afterwards, cap RocksDB with a rocksdb.config.setter using a shared block cache and WriteBufferManager.

In 4.3, processing.exception.handler applies only to regular stream tasks; an exception during global store or global KTable processing, here your addGlobalStore processor running on the global thread, does not reach it and goes to the uncaught exception handler. The default handler closes the client, which moves to ERROR, a terminal state. Restart the pods after the change, because ERROR does not recover on its own.

Where the bad records go: nowhere but the log. Dead letter queue support does not exist for global stores; for global store exceptions the record metadata is logged and the record is not sent to fx-dlq. Take topic, partition and offset from the handler's log lines and inspect fx-rates there.

Three changes are required and one plan step must go.

1. Replication policy on both connectors. Strimzi requires the same replication.policy.class (and separator) in sourceConnector and checkpointConnector; with the identity policy only on the source connector, replication or offset synchronization can fail. Add replication.policy.class: org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.IdentityReplicationPolicy under checkpointConnector.config.

3. Tasks. Each connector runs 1 task unless tasksMax is set, so with replicas: 3 the source connector would use one worker. Set sourceConnector.tasksMax, for example 12; the ceiling is the partition count, 480. Raise checkpointConnector.tasksMax if you have many groups.

A way back means removing legacy-to-nova first and then mirroring nova into a clean legacy, and should be tested before Monday.

reference:
Protect the topics in the manifests themselves, before anything moves. A pruned or deleted KafkaTopic resource is a deleted Kafka topic: the Topic Operator removes the topic when its managed KafkaTopic is deleted. PruneLast=true does not help; it only moves pruning to the end of the sync, and the resources are still deleted.

Add to every KafkaTopic, in platform/ first:

metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Prune=false,Delete=false

Prune=false on the resource overrides kafka-platform's prune: true, so a topic whose file disappears from that Application's path is shown as out of sync and not pruned; this also covers a file removed by mistake later. Delete=false keeps the topic when an Application that manages it is deleted, even with the resources finalizer.

Order:
1. Commit the annotations to platform/ and let kafka-platform sync them.
2. Create the team Applications (same repository, path teams/<team>/topics), then merge the commit that moves the files.
3. Check that each KafkaTopic's argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id now names its team Application, for example team-payments:kafka.strimzi.io/KafkaTopic:kafka/<name>.
4. Create kafka-cluster for the Kafka resource, then delete kafka-platform; for extra safety use argocd app delete kafka-platform --cascade=false.

If a KafkaTopic resource ever has to be renamed or removed without touching the topic, annotate it strimzi.io/managed: "false" first.

PruneLast is no protection: it only delays pruning to the last wave. Move the files, let the team Applications take the topics over and check that their argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id annotations name the team Applications. Then delete kafka-platform without cascade: argocd app delete kafka-platform --cascade=false, which removes the Application and keeps the Kafka resource and all topics; kafka-cluster then adopts prod.

Three things change.

1. TimeWindows.of(...).grace(...) was removed in 4.0; size and grace are now set together with TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace.
2. A windowed count updates continuously, which is why you got alerts at 5, 6, 7. suppress(Suppressed.untilWindowCloses(unbounded())) holds each window's result until the window closes and then emits the final count once; the >= 5 filter must come after it.
3. The key of a windowed KTable is Windowed<String>; unwrap it with key() and window() and write with explicit serdes.

KStream<String, AuthEvent> events =
    builder.stream("auth-events", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), authEventSerde));
events.filter((k, v) -> v.result() == Result.FAILED)
      .groupBy((k, v) -> v.userId(), Grouped.with(Serdes.String(), authEventSerde))
      .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(5), Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
      .count()
      .suppress(Suppressed.untilWindowCloses(unbounded()))
      .filter((windowedUser, count) -> count >= 5)
      .toStream()
      .map((windowedUser, count) -> KeyValue.pair(windowedUser.key(),
            windowedUser.window().start() + "," + count))
      .to("login-alerts", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()));

(unbounded() is the static buffer factory used in the Streams guide; cap it in production.)

Timing: a window closes when stream time passes its end plus the 1-minute grace. Stream time only advances when records arrive, so in a quiet period an alert waits for the next events.
correct_alternative:
Use the emit-on-close strategy instead of suppress; it keeps the window results in the RocksDB-backed store. On the windowed stream, before count(), call emitStrategy(...) with the "emit on window close" strategy (KIP-825):

events.filter((k, v) -> v.result() == Result.FAILED)
      .groupBy((k, v) -> v.userId(), Grouped.with(Serdes.String(), authEventSerde))
      .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(5), Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
      // emitStrategy(<emit on window close>) here
      .count()
      .filter((wk, count) -> count >= 5)
      .toStream()
      .map((wk, count) -> KeyValue.pair(wk.key(), String.valueOf(count)))
      .to("login-alerts", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()));

TimeWindows.of and grace() no longer exist in 4.x; ofSizeAndGrace replaces them. With the emit strategy the count is emitted once per window after it closes, so the filter sees only final counts. key() unwraps the windowed key. Closing depends on stream time (window end plus 1 minute grace), and stream time moves only when records arrive.

reference:
Parallelism: Kafka Streams creates one task per input partition of a subtopology, so the card-tx side has 48 tasks and at most 48 threads do work. The draft's 12 pods x 8 threads (96) would leave half idle; plan for example 12 pods x 4 threads, and scale by adding partitions to card-tx, not threads.

The join: card-tx (48) and card-profiles (12) are not co-partitioned, so a KStream-KTable join on them fails at runtime with a TopologyBuilderException. Two options:
- Repartition the smaller side up: card-profiles as a KTable via toStream().repartition(Repartitioned.numberOfPartitions(48)).toTable(), same default partitioner. Cost: one more topic and store, but state is split: about 24 GB active plus 24 GB standby, roughly 48 GB over all pods (4 GB per pod at 12 pods).
- GlobalKTable: no co-partitioning, but every pod holds and reads all 24 GB (about 288 GB at 12 pods) and every restart rebuilds it.
I would take the repartition.

Failover: with group.protocol=streams, num.standby.replicas in StreamsConfig is ignored, as are warm-up replicas; set kafka-configs.sh --alter --entity-type groups --entity-name card-risk --add-config streams.num.standby.replicas=1. A standby lets a task resume without replaying its changelog.

The 10-minute window store adds state per card active in a window; peak input is about 12 MB/s (15,000 x 800 bytes).

Numbers still needed: changelog restore throughput per pod and disk per pod (to check the one-minute target without a standby), the number of cards active per window, and the growth of card-profiles.
correct_alternative: Use a GlobalKTable for card-profiles: the GlobalKTable join needs no co-partitioning, so the 12 versus 48 partitions stop mattering, and lookups never cross pods. The price is that each pod keeps the full ~24 GB profile store and reads the whole topic; at 12 pods that is close to 288 GB of local state before RocksDB overhead, so fewer, larger pods are better, for example 8 pods x 6 threads, since only 48 card-tx tasks exist and threads beyond 48 in total would idle. Do not use the 96-thread draft. For the one-minute failover, the streams protocol ignores the client's num.standby.replicas; configure streams.num.standby.replicas=1 on the group with kafka-configs.sh --entity-type groups. I still need the restore speed of a pod's changelogs and the disk available per pod to confirm the target and the pod size.
generic: Kafka Streams scales horizontally, so run several instances on Kubernetes with enough CPU and memory. Use a KTable for the profiles and join it with the transaction stream, use standby replicas for fast failover, and monitor consumer lag. Choose the number of partitions and pods based on your throughput and test under load.
note: Computed points: m1 (48 tasks; draft 96 threads) and m6 (state, tolerance about 25 %). The guide's general rule is to repartition the smaller topic up to the larger count, while for stream-table joins it recommends repartitioning the KStream because repartitioning a KTable may create a second store (dsl-api.md:2112); here repartitioning the KStream down to 12 would cut parallelism to 12 tasks, which is the condition that is easy to invert; an answer that repartitions card-tx down to 12 is not given a must-not but misses m1's point about 48. The 4.3 upgrade guide repeats the streams-protocol notes (chunks 5f036a3e2ec96228, 47cfd76f6f4e07c0). covered_by_index is partly only because the restore rate and disk numbers are design inputs no page gives. reference:
I would put the CDC connectors into a new KafkaConnect, cdc-connect, and leave ingest-connect alone.

Why: exactly-once source support is a worker setting. On ingest-connect it needs two rolling updates of its 40 production connectors (exactly.once.source.support: preparing on every worker, then enabled). A new cluster starts with enabled, and failures or rebalances of the CDC connectors no longer touch the others. It needs its own groupId and config, offset and status topics, or it would join ingest-connect. Cost: more pods and another cluster to run.

Configuration:
- cdc-connect spec.config: exactly.once.source.support: enabled.
- Each CDC connector: exactly.once.support: required, so creation fails unless the plugin can provide exactly-once; keep transaction.boundary: poll unless the plugin documents connector-defined boundaries.
- KafkaUser ACLs, type transactionalId: Write and Describe on connect-cluster-cdc-connect and on cdc-connect-<connector>-0 for each connector, 31 IDs (1 + 30 x 1 task), or a prefix per connector; plus the usual topic and offsets-topic rights.
- Downstream: the guarantee only holds for readers using isolation.level=read_committed. Set consumer.override.isolation.level: read_committed on the 12 sink connectors (the default override policy All allows it) and isolation.level=read_committed in the Java consumers.

Trade-offs: transactions add latency; consumers see records only after commit.

Numbers still needed: bytes per second per database (2,000 changes/s says nothing about size), the latency consumers accept, how many tasks the plugin really starts, and whether the plugin version signals exactly-once support.
correct_alternative: Keeping everything on ingest-connect is possible. Roll its workers twice: first exactly.once.source.support: preparing on all six, then enabled; never jump straight to enabled on a running cluster. The trade-off is that the 40 existing connectors take part in both rolls and share failure domains with CDC. Mark each CDC connector exactly.once.support: required so a connector that cannot do it is rejected. Grant transactionalId ACLs in the ingest-connect KafkaUser: connect-cluster-ingest-connect and ingest-connect-<connector>-<task>, which is 31 IDs for 30 single-task connectors. Exactly-once in Kafka is only visible to readers in read_committed: sinks need consumer.override.isolation.level=read_committed and the Java services isolation.level=read_committed. Before sizing I need the bytes per second per database and the latency the consumers tolerate, since transaction.boundary (poll) decides how often records become visible.
generic: Kafka Connect supports exactly-once for source connectors. Enable it in the worker configuration, make sure your connectors support it, and use a separate Connect cluster if you need isolation. Monitor the connectors and test failure scenarios before going to production.
